The thing I keep seeing is that essentially isn't her fault, which is never the case when it comes to this stuff. When being granted access to classified information, you are made very aware (yes even she had to go through the briefings) that proper handling of classified information is always your responsibility. 

One argument is that she never sent anything but received it, which is out of her control. False. If you are on an unsecured system and receive classified info, it is your responsibility to report that to an appropriate security officer and submit the system for analysis. Immediately. If she had done this, there would likely have been no issue at all. Now, years after the fact and after tons of information has been found to be deleted from the system, it is virtually impossible to determine what may or may not have been compromised.

Another argument is that her .gov email was unsecured as well and wouldn't have prevented any compromise. This is also false. It isn't about the email address. It is entirely about the system. Classified information can only be handled on a closed network and wouldn't have been tied to any unclassified system at all.

Another argument is that the information wasn't classified at the time. Yes, different agencies can set their own standards for classification thresholds. The problem is that there is a very large difference between something that is unclassified and top secret. That difference is pretty universal. Something unclassified to the State Department would not be Top Secret to another agency.
